catalog_quote: Each phonemic word of more than one syllable carries a single primary stress. 2.1 Stress There is a suprasegmental item of stress which is considered to be phonemic. Its occurrence in any word is unpredictable but it identifies a syllable on which it falls as being one of the last three syllables of a word. On many occasions the position of primary stress / / is the minimal difference between a pair of words, e.g. gayáŋ 'a type of spear'; gáyaŋ 'crow'; ʔirít 'outskirts, edge'; ʔírit 'eggs of head-lice'; bawí 'repent'; báwi 'field shelter'; bokár 'wild pig'; bókar 'disperse' ... Furthermore, there is a feature of stress which is considered to be non-phonemic since its occurrence can always be predicted in terms of primary stress. This feature is termed secondary stress. ... sweep_summary: Central Bontoc is in the catalog as LEXICAL (Reid 1963, revised web copy: phonemic, unpredictable primary stress on one of the last three syllables). The sweep turned up a single title-keyword item, Thurgood 1997 'Bontok reduplication and prosodic templates' (Oceanic Linguistics 36(1):135-148, DOI 10.2307/3623073), already on our per-language bibliography and wishlist. It is closed on JSTOR with no open copy anywhere checked (Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, HathiTrust, archive.org, author pages); only the OpenAlex abstract was obtained and ( updated). The abstract concerns heavy-syllable reduplication, gemination, metathesis and prosodic-template copying and is silent on stress placement, so the item is classed prosody-but-not-word-stress, not-read, low priority. No new first-hand stress statement was read; the catalog's deciding source (Reid 1963, held and previously verified verbatim, with Reid 2005 and Aoyama & Reid 2006 already on file) stands unchanged.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Reid 1963 PDF/text at sec. 2 and sec. 2.1, pp. 2-3 of the revised copy, exactly as the locator says. (2) The source is a dedicated phonology article by the language's principal describer, based on two years of monolingual-village fieldwork, and its stress analysis (phonemic primary stress, unpredictable but within the last three syllables; length on stressed open penult/antepenult; predictable secondary stress) is restated unchanged in Reid 1976 (held), Reid 2005 (fetched sources now, confirms 'contrastive stress' in both the 1960 and 2004 phonemic systems), Reid 2007/2011 (held) and the Minpaku Talking Dictionary (held). (3) Glottolog's longer 'grammars' are a 1909 pre-phonemic grammar that Reid 2007 explicitly faults on accent/length, a 1932 study, and a 1970 discourse grammar; web search found no later stress/prosody or acoustic-stress study

sources.quote: 'For Central Bontok we are able to refer to the description in Reid (1963), which shows that forty years ago, the language had ... only fourteen consonant phonemes, four vowel phonemes and contrastive stress, as shown in Table 1.' Tables 1 and 2 both list 'V́ (Vowel stress)' as part of the phonemic system (1960 and 2004). No further detail on stress position; paper is about segmental change under contact.

sources.quote: Instrumental study of singleton/geminate consonant duration (10 speakers). Stress enters only as a stimulus control: 'Preferences were given to words that (1) consisted of two syllables, (2) had stress on the first syllable ...'. No statement on stress placement or its phonemic status.

sources.quote: This paper analyzes reduplication patterns in Bontok. ... The claim is that in Bontok heavy syllable reduplication interacts with two phonological processes: gemination and metathesis. It is suggested that these processes occur because there is a constraint preventing glottal stops from being introduced into syllable codas. It is also argued that in reduplication, not just the segmental structure is copied, but the prosodic template as well.

sources.note: Only other prosodic-phonology treatment of (Guinaang) Bontok located; may restate stress/length interaction with reduplication, but is built on Reid's data and unlikely to change the lexical/three-syllable-window coding.
